items.prompt: In L1, why did switching email providers touch 12 classes?
choices: The new provider changed twelve public method names
Each class chose the vendor itself
The old provider had to be deleted from twelve servers
items.explanation: Each of the 12 classes decided for itself which vendor to build, so the same decision existed twelve times.

items.prompt: Which two jobs were mixed inside each of the 12 classes?
choices: Using email and choosing the vendor
Reading orders and writing files
Sending email and deleting messages
items.explanation: Each class used email and also decided which concrete vendor to build.

items.prompt: Where should the vendor decision live after the fix?
choices: In every class, repeated with a comment
In a README listing the vendor name
In one place that wires up the program
items.explanation: Exactly one place decides; everything else just uses the result.

items.prompt: What was the risk of missing one of the 12 classes?
choices: The build would fail with a clear error
It would keep the old provider silently
It would send each email twice
items.explanation: A missed class compiles fine and silently keeps the old vendor.

items.prompt: Is the ripple caused by the vendor switch itself?
choices: No, by where the decision lived
Yes, every vendor switch ripples
Yes, because vendors change so often
items.explanation: The same switch is one edit if the decision lives in one place.

items.prompt: What did the tightly coupled classes name directly?
choices: A description of what email can do
A configuration file
A concrete vendor class
items.explanation: They wrote the vendor class name inside themselves.

items.prompt: Which fix did L1 say does not address the cause?
choices: Moving the decision into a single place
Searching harder for each construction site
Depending on a description of an email client
items.explanation: Searching harder still leaves 12 copies of the decision.

items.prompt: A reviewer sees `new AcmeMailClient()` inside a business class. What does it signal?
choices: The class took on the vendor decision
The class is already fully abstracted away
The class is fully covered by tests
items.explanation: Building the vendor inside means that class decides which one is used.

items.prompt: A team switches payment vendors and must edit 9 files that each build `new PayCoClient()`. What is the root cause?
choices: The new vendor has a more complicated API surface
Nine files is simply too few to organise well
The payment vendor changes its pricing too often
The vendor decision is copied into all 9 files
items.explanation: The same decision was copied into nine places. Any change to it must visit every copy, whatever the vendor or API.
items.reference:
Where the decision lives
before: 12 classes each decide the vendor
after: 1 place decides, 12 classes just use it
switching vendor: 12 edits versus 1 edit
Why: the ripple comes from where the vendor decision is allowed to live, not from the switch itself.
items.learnMore:
Why one decision rippled

Each class mixed two jobs: using email and choosing the vendor. The second job was copied into every class, so changing the decision meant changing every copy.

Common mistake

Blaming the search: being more careful about finding every construction site does not remove the duplication.
items.reflection: Think of a fact your team copied into many places (a URL, a limit, a name). What would it take to make it live in exactly one?

items.prompt: After a refactor, 11 of 12 classes receive the email client from outside, but one still builds `new AcmeMailClient()` internally. What happens on the provider switch?
choices: Nothing breaks, because eleven of twelve is fully covered
That one class silently keeps using the old provider
The build fails, because two providers cannot coexist
All twelve classes pick up the new provider automatically
items.explanation: A leftover construction site still decides for itself, so it keeps the old vendor with no error.

A class is too large and needs to be split into smaller ones

items.explanation: The other options describe Single responsibility, Liskov and interface segregation failures. The ripple is business logic bound to a concrete vendor.

Scripts cannot rewrite a constructor call in source code
It would only work for exactly twelve classes in total

items.prompt: Which principle says a class should have one reason to change?
choices: Interface segregation
Dependency inversion
Single responsibility
items.explanation: S is about one reason to change, not several.

items.prompt: Which principle is about depending on an abstraction rather than a concrete class?
choices: Liskov substitution
Dependency inversion
Single responsibility
items.explanation: D is the dependency principle.

items.prompt: Which principle says not to force classes to depend on methods they never use?
choices: Interface segregation
Open/closed
Single responsibility
items.explanation: I is about narrow, focused shapes.

items.prompt: Which principle says a stand-in must be safe wherever the original was expected?
choices: Interface segregation
Single responsibility
Liskov substitution
items.explanation: L is about safe substitution.

items.prompt: Which principle says to add behavior without editing code that already works?
choices: Liskov substitution
Open/closed
Interface segregation
items.explanation: O means open for extension, closed for modification.

items.prompt: What does the S in SOLID stand for?
choices: Single responsibility
Safe substitution
Strict type separation
items.explanation: The first letter is Single responsibility.

items.prompt: Which principle did the 12-file email ripple mainly violate?
choices: Single responsibility
Liskov substitution
Dependency inversion
items.explanation: Classes were wired directly to one concrete vendor.

items.prompt: Should every SOLID principle be applied to every refactor?
choices: Yes, apply all five together every time
No, match the principle to the symptom
Yes, but only in the order S, O, L, I, D
items.explanation: Each principle addresses a different failure mode.

items.prompt: A test double must define `scheduleSend`, `trackOpens` and `manageUnsubscribeList` even though the code under test only calls `send`. Which principle is being broken?
choices: Open/closed
Single responsibility
Dependency inversion
Interface segregation
items.explanation: The double is forced to provide methods nobody calls because the shape it must satisfy is too big.
items.reference:
Symptom to principle
unrelated reasons to change: S
new variant forces edits to old code: O
stand-in fits shape, breaks callers: L
forced to stub unused methods: I
logic names a vendor class directly: D
Why: each principle names one kind of failure; match the symptom first, then pick the fix.
items.learnMore:
Reading symptoms

The five principles are not a checklist applied everywhere. Each one describes a failure you can observe, and the L1 ripple is specifically about what a class depends on.

Common mistake

Reaching for single responsibility whenever a change touches many files. Many files can be a dependency problem, not a size problem.
items.reflection: Think of a recurring pain in a system you know. Which symptom row does it match, and which fix would you have wrongly reached for first?

items.prompt: Adding a new report format forces you to edit an existing `if/else` chain in a class that works well today. Which principle is the best fit?
choices: Dependency inversion
Liskov substitution
Open/closed
Interface segregation
items.explanation: New behavior should arrive as new code, not as edits to existing working code. That is open/closed.

items.prompt: What is dependency injection?
choices: Passing a dependency in from outside
Building the dependency inside the class
Deleting the dependency from the code
items.explanation: Injection means the class receives its dependency, usually via its constructor.

items.prompt: After inversion, what does OrderService depend on?
choices: AcmeMailClient and BoltMailClient
A description of an email client
The composition root and tests
items.explanation: It depends on what an email client can do, not on a vendor.

items.prompt: What is the composition root?
choices: The largest class in the whole codebase
A test suite that checks every dependency
The one place that wires classes together
items.explanation: It is the single assembly point near program startup.

items.prompt: Where does the vendor choice live after DIP?
choices: In one place, where it is wired
Nowhere, it simply disappears
Inside each of the consumer classes
items.explanation: The decision is concentrated, not removed.

items.prompt: How many consumer classes change to add a third provider after DIP?
choices: One in each consumer
None
Half of them
items.explanation: Consumers stay unchanged; only the root picks the new class.

items.prompt: What can you hand to OrderService in a test?
choices: A fake honoring the same contract
Only the real vendor client class
Nothing, tests cannot inject
items.explanation: Any object satisfying the contract can be injected.

items.prompt: In the diagram, what do the vendor classes do after inversion?
choices: They call OrderService
They are removed from the code
They implement the abstraction
items.explanation: Each vendor class satisfies the EmailClient contract.

items.prompt: What does 'inversion' refer to?
choices: Reversing the order of method calls
The direction of dependency arrows
Turning classes into functions
items.explanation: Vendors used to be pointed at; now they point at the abstraction.

items.prompt: After dependency inversion, a third provider is added. Where does the choice to use it get made?
choices: Inside OrderService, in a new branch
Inside the abstraction itself, when it is loaded
In every class that sends an email
In the composition root that builds OrderService
items.explanation: Consumers never name vendors, so the only place that needs to know the new class exists is the one that wires the program.
items.reference:
What inverting moves
before: OrderService points at AcmeMailClient
after: OrderService points at EmailClient (abstraction)
vendor classes point at the abstraction too
the vendor choice moves to the composition root
Why: the dependency arrow now points at an abstraction owned by the business logic, and the concrete choice is made in one place.
items.learnMore:
What changes structurally

Business logic stops naming vendors. Vendor classes satisfy a contract the business logic defined, and whoever assembles the program picks which one is passed in.

Common mistake

Thinking the decision vanished. It moved to the composition root, and exactly one place now makes it.
items.reflection: Think of a plug and socket you use daily. Which side defines the shape, and what would break if every appliance had its wiring fixed into the wall?

Only half fixed, because a hidden vendor dependency remains
Tests are impossible, since mocks need the real client too
items.explanation: The helper still names the vendor, so a switch must still visit this class. Injection has to be followed through.

items.prompt: When is an abstraction worth adding?
choices: Whenever any new class is created
When the concrete choice may vary
Only in very large projects
items.explanation: Likely variation or a real test need pays back its cost.

items.prompt: What does an unnecessary abstraction cost?
choices: An extra file and a layer
Nothing, it is completely free
All of the existing tests
items.explanation: It is indirection with nothing to buy back.

items.prompt: A fixed tax formula has one implementation. Abstraction?
choices: Always needed
Needed only in tests
Not needed yet
items.explanation: No variation, so no payback.

items.prompt: A test must avoid a slow real network call. Abstraction?
choices: Never worth the effort
Yes, a fake can stand in
Only if the call is fast
items.explanation: A test need is a real reason.

items.prompt: When should a second tax jurisdiction trigger an abstraction?
choices: When it actually appears
Years before it could appear
Never, copy the class instead
items.explanation: Add the abstraction when the second variant exists.

items.prompt: Is 'we might switch vendors someday' enough on its own?
choices: Yes, that is always enough on its own
No, vendors never change
It is weak without evidence
items.explanation: A real, likely variation is stronger than a vague maybe.

items.prompt: What keeps DIP from being over-applied?
choices: Asking what pays the cost back
Adding even more layers of code
Banning all interfaces
items.explanation: Cost versus payback keeps it honest.

items.prompt: Which is a good reason to inject a database driver?
choices: Drivers are objects in the language
Backends could be swapped or faked
It simply looks tidy
items.explanation: Swappable or fakeable dependencies justify the seam.

items.prompt: A utility formats dates with one fixed rule and no second format is planned. A teammate wants a `DateFormatter` interface 'for flexibility'. What is the best response?
choices: Accept it, since interfaces are always free to add
Add it, but only if it has a unit test
Replace the utility with a database setting
Decline now, add it when a second format is needed
items.explanation: Nothing pays back the extra layer today. A real second format will show what the abstraction should look like.
items.reference:
Pay only when it buys something
swappable vendor or backend: yes
test needs a fake of a slow call: yes
fixed formula, one implementation: no
imagined second variant: not yet
Why: an abstraction costs a file and a layer; add it when a real variation or test need pays that back.
items.learnMore:
The cost side of DIP

Every abstraction is something a reader has to follow. It is justified where the concrete choice is likely to vary or a test genuinely needs a substitute.

Common mistake

Adding interfaces everywhere 'just in case'. Wait for a concrete reason and let it shape the abstraction.
items.reflection: Think of an abstraction in a project you know that never gained a second implementation. What would you have lost by waiting until it did?

items.prompt: Which case most clearly justifies introducing an abstraction right away?
choices: A rate-limited third-party API that tests must not hit
A class sorts a list with one standard comparison rule
A constant holds the number of days in a week
A function adds two integers
items.explanation: The slow, external dependency needs a fake in tests, which is a concrete payoff.

items.prompt: What does Liskov substitution require of a stand-in?
choices: It behaves as callers expect
It has the same class name
It is written by the same team
items.explanation: A safe stand-in keeps the behavior the original promised.

items.prompt: What does `sent: true` mean to callers of `send()`?
choices: The email really went out
The email was logged only
The email waits in a queue
items.explanation: Callers treat it as a promise of delivery.

items.prompt: NullEmailClient reports `sent: false`. Is it safe to inject?
choices: No, it returns an object
Yes, it tells the truth
No, it has no real vendor
items.explanation: Honest reporting preserves the contract.

items.prompt: LogOnlyEmailClient logs and returns `sent: true`. What is the problem?
choices: It lies about delivery
It prints too much text
It is far too fast
items.explanation: It claims success for an email that was never sent.

items.prompt: Does a matching method signature guarantee safe substitution?
choices: No, behavior must match too
Yes, always
Yes, if the names match exactly
items.explanation: Shape alone says nothing about what results mean.

items.prompt: Who is hurt when a stand-in lies about success?
choices: Nobody, it is harmless
Callers that trust the result
Only the compiler
items.explanation: Callers act on a false belief.

items.prompt: Which stand-in is safest when sending is disabled?
choices: One that reports not sent
One that throws a random error
One that reports sent anyway
items.explanation: A truthful 'not sent' lets callers react correctly.

items.prompt: What does a type system usually check about a stand-in?
choices: The shape only
The behavior as well
Both fully
items.explanation: Types check signatures, not what results mean.

items.prompt: A `CachedEmailClient` returns `sent: true` immediately but only queues the message and may drop it on restart. Is it a safe substitute?
choices: Yes, because it returns the same result shape
Yes, since queueing is a common technique
No, because it must also implement scheduling
No, it promises delivery it cannot guarantee
items.explanation: Callers read `sent: true` as delivered. A queue that can drop messages breaks that promise even though the shape matches.
items.reference:
Shape versus promise
shape: has send(), returns { sent }
promise: sent true means it really went out
NullEmailClient: sent false, honest, safe
LogOnlyEmailClient: sent true after logging, a lie
Why: a stand-in is substitutable only if it keeps the behavior callers rely on, not just the method names.
items.learnMore:
The behavioral contract

A signature says what can be called. The contract also says what the result means. Callers build decisions on that meaning, so a stand-in that bends it is unsafe even when it type-checks.

Common mistake

Equating 'implements the interface' with 'safe to substitute'. Both must hold.
items.reflection: Think of something that looks like a drop-in replacement but behaves differently (a charger, a library, a coworker's template). What promise did it quietly break?

items.prompt: Which change would make `LogOnlyEmailClient` safe to inject?
choices: Rename the class to NullEmailClient
Return `sent: false` with a reason
Add a second method that logs more
Have it extend AcmeMailClient
items.explanation: Reporting truthfully makes the stand-in match what callers rely on. Names, extra methods and inheritance do not.

items.prompt: Two stand-ins have identical signatures. One throws when the address is invalid, like the real client; the other returns `sent: true` for any input. Which is the Liskov-safe one?
choices: The one that returns `sent: true` for any input
Neither, since both have the same signature
Both, since the signatures are identical
The one that throws on an invalid address
items.explanation: The real client's behavior on bad input is part of the contract. A stand-in that accepts everything hides failures callers expect.

items.prompt: Why can a type checker not catch a Liskov violation like LogOnlyEmailClient?
choices: Because it only checks signatures, not meaning
Because the class is declared in a separate file
Because return values are never type-checked at all
Because logging is a runtime-only feature
items.explanation: The violation lives in what `sent: true` means, which a signature cannot express.
items.reference:
Shape versus promise
shape: has send(), returns { sent }
promise: sent true means it really went out
NullEmailClient: sent false, honest, safe
LogOnlyEmailClient: sent true after logging, a lie
Why: a stand-in is substitutable only if it keeps the behavior callers rely on, not just the method names.
items.learnMore:
The behavioral contract

A signature says what can be called. The contract also says what the result means. Callers build decisions on that meaning, so a stand-in that bends it is unsafe even when it type-checks.

Common mistake

Equating 'implements the interface' with 'safe to substitute'. Both must hold.
items.reflection: Think of something that looks like a drop-in replacement but behaves differently (a charger, a library, a coworker's template). What promise did it quietly break?

items.prompt: What does interface segregation advise?
choices: Depend only on the methods you use
Put every method in one interface
Never use interfaces at all
items.explanation: Narrow, focused shapes beat one fat shape.

items.prompt: OrderService only calls `send()`. Which shape should it name?
choices: A narrow one with just send
The vendor class directly
A fat one with every feature
items.explanation: It should name only the capability it uses.

items.prompt: What goes wrong if a test fake must satisfy a fat shape?
choices: It becomes a real vendor
It needs stubs nobody calls
It runs faster
items.explanation: Unused stubs are the cost of a fat shape.

items.prompt: Can one class implement several narrow shapes?
choices: Yes, nothing forbids it
No, only one
Only inside tests
items.explanation: Segregation only stops forcing unused capabilities.

items.prompt: Which is a sign of a fat interface?
choices: Implementers leave methods empty
Every method is used by every caller
It has exactly one method
items.explanation: Empty stubs show forced capabilities.

items.prompt: What does ScheduledCampaignClient offer in L3?
choices: Only the ability to track opens
Both sending and scheduling
Nothing beyond tracking
items.explanation: A real campaign provider supports both narrow shapes.

items.prompt: Which SOLID letter is interface segregation?
choices: I
L
D
items.explanation: The fourth letter, I.

items.prompt: Does OrderService need to know `Schedulable` exists?
choices: No, it never schedules
Yes, to call send
Yes, to build the fake
items.explanation: A consumer depends only on what it calls.

items.prompt: A `SmsClient` is forced to implement `trackOpens` and `manageUnsubscribeList` because the abstraction requires them. It throws 'not supported' in both. What is the best fix?
choices: Make them return `sent: true` so callers are happy
Split the shape so SmsClient offers what it can
Delete SmsClient and use only the largest provider
Leave it, since throwing is a documented behavior
items.explanation: The shape asks for capabilities some implementers do not have. Narrow shapes remove the need for fake support.
items.reference:
Narrow shapes
fat shape: send + scheduleSend + trackOpens + unsubscribe
OrderService needs only: send
fake client forced to stub 3 unused methods
split: Sendable, Schedulable, Trackable, Unsubscribable
Why: depend on the narrow capability you use; classes can still implement several narrow shapes.
items.learnMore:
Why narrow shapes

A big shape drags every implementer and every test double into providing capabilities they do not have. Depending only on what you call keeps substitution cheap.

Common mistake

Thinking splitting forbids one class from doing many things. A class may implement several narrow shapes; no consumer is forced to depend on all of them.
items.reflection: Think of a form or API that asked you for far more than you needed. What would the narrow version have looked like?

items.prompt: `OrderService` is changed to require the fat `FullFeaturedEmailClient`. What is the first practical consequence for tests?
choices: The fake needs three stubs that nothing calls
The service stops calling send completely
The composition root is no longer needed
The vendor classes become impossible to inject
items.explanation: Anything handed to the service must now satisfy the whole shape, including capabilities it never uses.

items.prompt: A marketing client supports sending and scheduling. After splitting, how should `OrderService` see it?
choices: As a Schedulable, since that is its richest capability
As a FullFeaturedEmailClient, to keep one type
As a Trackable, because tracking is the next step
As a Sendable only, since that is all it calls
items.explanation: The consumer depends on the narrow capability it uses; the client may offer more without the consumer knowing.

items.prompt: Which statement about splitting a fat interface is correct?
choices: It forbids a class from implementing several shapes
It ensures that no class has more than one method
It requires a separate interface for each single method
It stops forcing implementers to provide unused methods
items.explanation: Splitting is about what consumers must depend on, not about limiting what a class may offer.
